items.title: The World's Destruction: Beings Depart, Then Seven Suns Burn Away the Earth

items.zh: 於最後增已，爾時那落迦有情唯沒不生。如是漸漸乃至沒盡，當知說名那落迦世間壞。如那落迦壞，傍生、餓鬼壞亦如是。爾時人中隨一有情，自然法爾所得第二靜慮。其餘有情展轉隨學，亦復如是。皆此沒已，生極淨光天眾同分中。當知爾時說名人世間壞。如人趣既爾，天趣亦然。
items.en: After the final increase, beings in hell then only pass away and are no longer born there; gradually, until they are entirely gone, this is called the destruction of the hell-world. As with hell, so with the animal and hungry-ghost worlds. At that time, some one being among humans spontaneously attains the second dhyāna; the rest, in turn, learn to do likewise. All of them, upon passing away, are reborn among the multitude of the Radiant Light heaven. This is called the destruction of the human world; and as with humans, so too with the heavenly realms below.

items.zh: 當於此時，五趣世間居住之處無一有情可得，所有資具亦不可得。非唯資具不可復得，爾時天雨亦不可得。由無雨故，大地所有藥草叢林皆悉枯槁。復由無雨之所攝故，令此日輪熱勢增大。又諸有情能感壞劫業增上力故，及依六種所燒事故，復有六日輪漸次而現。彼諸日輪望舊日輪所有熱勢，踰前四倍。既成七已，熱遂增七。
items.en: At this time, not a single being remains anywhere in the dwelling-places of the five realms, nor can any of life's requisites be found. Not only can requisites no longer be found — even rain no longer falls from the sky. Because there is no rain, all the plants and forests of the earth wither away entirely. And because there is no rain, the heat of the sun grows ever greater. Further, through the dominant force of beings' karma capable of bringing about this eon of destruction, and depending on six things yet to be burned, six further suns gradually appear, one after another; each one's heat, compared to the original sun's, exceeds it fourfold. Once seven suns stand in the sky, the heat has thus intensified through seven stages.
What are the six things that are burned up?

items.zh: 一、小大溝坑，由第二日輪之所枯竭；二、小河大河，由第三日輪之所枯竭；三、無熱大池、由第四日輪之所枯竭；四者、大海，由第五日輪及第六一分之所枯竭；五、蘇迷盧山及以大地，體堅實故，由第六一分及第七日輪之所燒然。即此火焰為風所鼓，展轉熾盛、極至梵世。
items.en: First, all the small and large pools and pits are dried up by the second sun. Second, the small and great rivers are dried up by the third sun. Third, the great lake of no heat is dried up by the fourth sun. Fourth, the great oceans are dried up by the fifth sun and part of the sixth. Finally, Mount Sumeru and the great earth itself, being of solid substance, are burned away by the remaining part of the sixth sun together with the seventh. This flame, fanned by the wind, blazes on and on, reaching all the way up to the Brahmā world.

items.zh: 又如是等，略為三事。一、水所生事、謂藥草等，由初所槁；二、即水事、由五所涸；三、恒相續住體堅實事，由二所燒。
items.en: Further, these can be summarised as three kinds of thing: first, things that grow from water, such as medicinal herbs, which are withered by the first sun; second, water itself, which is dried up by the fifth; third, things whose substance is solid and continues unbroken, which are burned by the remaining two.

items.title: Water and Wind: The Larger Cycle of Destruction

items.zh: 如是世界皆悉燒已，乃至灰墨及與餘影皆不可得，廣說如經。從此名為器世間已壞。滿足二十中劫。如是壞已，復二十中劫住。
items.en: Thus, once the world has been entirely burned away, not even ash or any trace of it can be found — as explained at length in the sūtras. From this point, the physical world is said to have been destroyed. This fills out twenty intermediate eons. Once thus destroyed, a further twenty intermediate eons of emptiness follow.

items.zh: 云何水災？謂過七火災已，於第二靜慮中，有俱生水界起，壞器世間，如水消鹽。此之水界與器世間一時俱沒。如是沒已，復二十中劫住。
items.en: What is the calamity of water? After seven fire-calamities have passed, within the second dhyāna heaven, an innate water element arises, destroying the physical world there as water dissolves salt. This water element and that world vanish together at one and the same time. Once thus vanished, a further twenty intermediate eons of emptiness follow.

items.zh: 云何風災？謂七水災過已，復七火災；從此無間，於第三靜慮中有俱生風界起，壞器世間，如風乾支節、復能消盡。此之風界與器世間一時俱沒。所以者何？現見有一由風界發，乃令其骨皆悉消盡。從此壞已，復二十中劫住。
items.en: What is the calamity of wind? After seven water-calamities have passed, seven more fire-calamities occur; immediately following these, within the third dhyāna heaven, an innate wind element arises, destroying the physical world there, as wind dries out the body's joints and wastes them entirely away. This wind element and that world vanish together at one and the same time. Why is this so? It is observed that when the wind element becomes active in illness, it can waste even the bones away entirely. From this destruction, a further twenty intermediate eons of emptiness follow.

items.title: The Sixteenth Power Begins: The World's Formation

items.zh: 如是略說世間已壞。云何世間成？謂過如是二十中劫已，一切有情業增上力故，世間復成。爾時最初於虛空中，第三靜慮器世間成。如第三靜慮，第二及初亦復如是。
items.en: Thus has the world's destruction been briefly explained. What now is the world's formation? After these twenty intermediate eons of emptiness have passed, through the dominant force of the collective karma of all beings, the world is formed once again. At that time, first of all, within empty space, the physical world of the third dhyāna comes into being. As with the third dhyāna, so too, in turn, with the second and the first.

items.zh: 爾時第三災頂有諸有情由壽盡故，業盡故，福盡故，從彼沒已，生第三靜慮。
items.en: At that time, beings at the peak of the third calamity, whose lifespan, karma, and merit have all been exhausted, pass away from there and are reborn in the third dhyāna.
In every other place it proceeds gradually in the same way.

items.title: Mahābrahmā's Wish, and the Desire-Realm Heavens

items.zh: 復從第二災頂生第二靜慮。餘一切處，應知亦爾。復從第一災頂，有一有情由壽等盡故，從彼沒已，生初靜慮梵世界中，為最大梵。由獨一故、而懷不悅。便有希望：今當云何令餘有情亦來生此。當發心時，諸餘有情由壽等盡故，從第二靜慮沒已，生初靜慮彼同分中。
items.en: Then, from the peak of the second calamity, beings are reborn in the second dhyāna, and it should be understood that this holds in the same way for every remaining level. Then, from the peak of the first calamity, one being, its lifespan and the rest having been exhausted, passes away from there and is reborn in the Brahmā world of the first dhyāna, becoming Mahābrahmā. Being alone, it feels displeased, and this wish arises: "How shall I now bring other beings to be born here as well?" At the very moment this wish arises, other beings, their lifespan and the rest having been exhausted, pass away from the second dhyāna and are reborn as this being's companions in the first dhyāna.

items.zh: 如是下三靜慮器及有情世間成已。於虛空中，欲界四天宮殿漸成。當知彼諸虛空宮殿皆如化出。又諸有情，從極淨光天眾同分沒，而來生此諸宮殿中。
items.en: Once the physical and living worlds of the lower three dhyānas have thus formed, the palaces of the four heavens of the desire realm gradually form within empty space; it should be understood that these palaces all arise as if by transformation. And beings come to be born in these palaces, having passed away from the multitude of the Radiant Light heaven.
The rest is as explained before.

blocks.text: Yesterday the human lifespan rose and fell within the eon of abiding. Today the world itself ends and begins again. Notice the order. The world does not end in catastrophe for its inhabitants: first all beings leave, rising through meditation to a higher realm, and only then do the seven suns burn the empty world. Formation then runs in exactly the reverse order.

Several short passages are missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours): 0286b04, the question "What are the six things burned?"; 0286b10–b13, which sums them up as three (what grows from water, such as herbs, withered by the first sun; water itself, dried by the fifth; and the solid, enduring things, burned by the second); 0286c03, "elsewhere it is the same, in sequence"; and 0286c13, "the rest is as explained before".

subs.head: The world empties before it burns

blocks.text: After the last increase in the human lifespan, beings in hell die and are no longer born there, until hell is empty; then the animal and ghost realms empty in the same way. Among humans, one being "spontaneously attains the second dhyāna; the rest, in turn, learn to do likewise", and all are reborn in the Radiant Light heaven (光音天, *Ābhāsvara*). The same happens in the lower heavens. Only when no being remains anywhere below the second dhyāna does the destruction proper begin.

Venerable Miào Jìng answers an obvious question: if everyone has become good, why is the world destroyed? "The eon of destruction destroys the world; it doesn't make the beings themselves suffer." The karma that sustains the world has a span, and when it is spent the world ends, just as Day 8 said: the world lasts "neither more nor less" than its karma allows.

With no beings, no rain falls; plants wither. Then a second sun appears and dries the pools; a third, the rivers; a fourth, the great Lake of No Heat (無熱惱池, *Anavatapta*); a fifth and part of the sixth, the oceans; the rest of the sixth and the seventh burn Mount Sumeru and the earth, up to the Brahmā heavens, until "not even ash or any trace of it can be found". Twenty intermediate eons of destruction are followed by twenty of emptiness.

After seven fire calamities comes one of water, arising within the second dhyāna and dissolving its world "as water dissolves salt". After seven such cycles of seven fires and one water, seven more fires, and then the first wind calamity, which wastes the third dhyāna "as wind dries out the body's joints". Both teachers work out the arithmetic: the first wind calamity comes in the sixty-fourth great eon.
The similes come from the body, which fits Day 9's point that outer calamities mirror inner states.

"First of all, within empty space, the physical world of the third dhyāna comes into being", then the second and the first. Master Cháng Bǎi: formation runs in exact reverse of destruction, from the top down. The first inhabitants of each newly formed level are beings from the level above whose lifespan, karma, and merit are exhausted. Both teachers identify "the peak of the first calamity" as the second dhyāna, since fire reaches only through the first.

One being from the second dhyāna is reborn as **Mahābrahmā** (大梵天王) in the empty first dhyāna. Alone, he grows displeased and wishes for company; at once other beings are reborn there as his ministers and multitude. Master Cháng Bǎi, as summarised in Ru-Yi's reading note, sees a quiet irony here: the being whom later traditions took for an all-powerful creator is simply the first to arrive, and his wish coincides with the arrival of others who were due to come by their own karma. It does not cause it.

The desire-realm heavens then form, and their palaces are filled by beings from the Radiant Light heaven, not from the first dhyāna. Venerable Miào Jìng explains why: the first dhyāna and the desire realm are burned together, lie empty together, and form together.

quiz.q: In the eon of destruction, how does the human world come to be "destroyed"?
options: humans are burned to death by fire
humans all fall into hell
one human spontaneously attains the second dhyāna, the rest learn to do likewise, and all are reborn in the Radiant Light heaven — the human world empties, and this is called its destruction
humans all migrate to other world-systems
quiz.why: "Some one being among humans spontaneously attains the second dhyāna; the rest, in turn, learn to do likewise. All of them, upon passing away, are reborn among the multitude of the Radiant Light heaven. This is called the destruction of the human world." The beings leave first and the world burns afterwards — as Venerable Miào Jìng says, the great calamities do not destroy beings. He notes that the Radiant Light heaven is the older translations' "Ābhāsvara," in the second dhyāna.

quiz.q: The seven suns dry up different waters in turn. What does the fourth sun dry up?
options: the great Lake of No Heat
the small and great rivers
the great oceans
the small and large pools and pits
quiz.why: The second sun dries the pools and pits (D), the third the rivers (B), the fourth "the great lake of no heat," the fifth and part of the sixth the oceans (C), and the rest of the sixth with the seventh burns Mount Sumeru and the earth. Master Cháng Bǎi: only once every drop of water is gone can fire consume even what seems most permanent.

quiz.q: By the eon of destruction, beings have all become good and been reborn in the second dhyāna. Why is the world still destroyed? According to Venerable Miào Jìng —
options: because some people secretly do evil
because Mahābrahmā grows angry
the eon of destruction is not a punishment — it destroys only the world, causing beings no suffering; the karma sustaining the world has a time-span, and when it is up, it ends
because the world was only an illusion
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The eon of destruction destroys the world; it doesn't make you suffer, it doesn't make the beings themselves suffer"; "but that karma has a time-span; when the time comes, the karma ends." This echoes §21: the karma that forms the world "is fixed in its power to sustain it for a full eon — neither more nor less." A and B mistake destruction for punishment.

quiz.q: What similes does the treatise use for how the water and wind calamities destroy the physical world?
options: water like fire burning wood, wind like water dissolving salt
both like a great fire
water like tides, wind like a typhoon
water "as water dissolves salt"; wind "as wind dries out the body's joints and wastes them entirely away"
quiz.why: Water destroys the world "as water dissolves salt"; wind destroys it "as wind dries out the body's joints and wastes them entirely away," because "it is observed that when the wind element becomes active in illness, it can waste even the bones away entirely." A swaps the similes. In both, the element "and that world vanish together at one and the same time."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, when the world forms again, which physical world forms first?
options: the physical world of the third dhyāna, within empty space, first; then the second and the first
the four human continents
the hells
the six desire-realm heavens
quiz.why: "At that time, first of all, within empty space, the physical world of the third dhyāna comes into being. As with the third dhyāna, so too, in turn, with the second and the first." Master Cháng Bǎi: formation runs in exact reverse of destruction — the last to fall is the first to reappear. C comes at the very end: as Venerable Miào Jìng says, the unhappy realms appear only after humans do evil.

quiz.q: Mahābrahmā, alone and displeased, wishes for company, and at once other beings are reborn in the first dhyāna. According to Master Cháng Bǎi, what is this passage showing?
options: that Mahābrahmā truly is the creator
that Mahābrahmā is merely the first to arrive; his wish happens to coincide with others' arrival, already due by their own karma, without causing it — later traditions mistook him for a creator
that wishes can summon anyone
that all first-dhyāna beings are Mahābrahmā's sons
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi (in the Ru-Yi reading note) sees the quiet irony: this figure, later mistaken by some traditions for an all-powerful creator, is simply the first being to arrive, whose private wish happens to coincide with — but does not cause — the arrival of others already due for rebirth there by their own karma. The text says that when the wish arose, other beings, "their lifespan and the rest having been exhausted," were reborn there — that is why they came. Venerable Miào Jìng: Mahābrahmā believed they came because of his thought and took himself as their father, and they agreed — D is exactly that misconception.
